reasons.specificity: It closely tracks the article’s section-by-section progression from Benjamin through Simmel, Marx, Schumpeter, myth cycles, and the neoliberal conclusion.
reasons.anchoring: Nearly all quotations occur and support the stated local turns, though the claim of “ontological equivalence” exceeds passages framed as affinity, analogy, and paradox.
reasons.non_obviousness: It usefully identifies ring composition, interrogatives as hinges, unequal focal positions, and the tension between recurrent cycles and terminal breakdown.
reasons.coherence: The reading and ledger largely agree about sequence and viewpoint, but the move from strategic analogy to allegedly literal religious language strains its own account.
reasons.usefulness: The extensive ledger is navigable with the text open, but the response is not one page and omits the requested sequence–effect and perspective–evidence tables.
reasons.hallucination_risk: Most claims are textually grounded, but intentional claims about the title’s question mark and the description of money and God as ontologically equivalent are insufficiently warranted.

decisive_errors.claim: “Religious language intensifies from analogy to ontological equivalence.”
decisive_errors.counter_passage: Deutschmann repeatedly qualifies the relation as an “inner affinity,” says money’s place is “not very far from” religion’s, and explicitly distinguishes capitalist myths from traditional religious myths; shared grounding in “trust” or “faith” does not establish ontological equivalence.

score.one_line: A highly source-specific and insightful narratological reading whose main weaknesses are overstatement of the religion analogy and failure to deliver the requested one-page tabular format.
